turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Ag, sorry we're late. The boom at the parking was stuck, and the robot on Main was out.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shame, that's not on you. Come sit. Howzit, was the rest of the morning alright?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I'm tired already and that waiting room is too loud. I nearly turned around.
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We left the flat in good time, doctor. She just sat there and wouldn't put the belt on.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Don't narrate my life. I'm not a child.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright, no fuss. What brought you in today, in your own words?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): My daughter brought me. I didn't ask for this appointment.
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been up half the night again. The whole flat hears it.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): Up with what? Tell me what's actually been happening.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): It's these cramps. My calves cramp at night and they wake me. Proper knots, like someone's wringing the muscle.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tell me a bit more. Both legs or one, and how long has it been going on?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, both calves. About two months. Mostly once I'm in bed, and sometimes a second one if I stretch the wrong way.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): And what do you do when it hits?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): I get up and walk it off on the cold floor. Most nights, ja.
[SEG0015] person_4 (NURSE): Sorry doctor, quick one. Vitals from just now. Blood pressure one forty eight over eighty six, pulse seventy eight.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, sister. Any chest pain with this, or feeling short of breath?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Chest is fine. Breathing's fine. Don't add stuff.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the feet, any numbness or pins and needles?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Feet are fine.
[SEG0020] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She hardly drinks, doctor. She reckons a bit of tea is enough for the day.
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): It's two cups. Don't make me sound daft.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): So in a whole day, what fluid are you actually taking?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Two cups of tea. Water tastes like nothing. I can't be bothered with it.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you on these days?
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): The water tablet. Frusemide, forty milligrams, one in the morning, for the blood pressure. Years now.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And she got magnesuim from the chemist. Big bottle, sits on the counter.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Magnesium, hey. Was that for the cramps? Do you know the dose?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Two tablets at night. Umm, I think maybe 250 milligrams each. Writing's tiny, I'm not a hundred percent sure.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else at all? Pain tablets, something for cholesterol?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): No. They offered me another one once and I never started it. Just these two.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): How's your energy through the day, if you had to put words to it?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Ag, by lunch I feel like a wet rag, proper finished. When it started, last winter or the one before, I can't date it.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She nods off in the chair after lunch. I'm not fighting her on the dates.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Earlier the feet were fine, you said. Anything else you've noticed in the legs?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Well, actually, when I get up for the cramp my feet feel dead. Like they're not mine for a minute, then it comes back.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Alright. Can I feel the calves quickly?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Ja. They're sore today so don't dig your thumb in.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Soft, no swelling, and the pulses are there in both feet. Tender both calves, not hot, not red.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): So what's the story. I haven't got all afternoon.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): I think these night cramps may be the water tablet pulling your potassium down, with so little to drink on top. I can't be sure till we see the blood.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should she stop the magnesuim then?
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, carry on with it. And before bed, gentle calf stretches, about twenty seconds each side, no bouncing.
[SEG0043] person_1 (PATIENT): Twenty seconds. I'm not joining some exercise class.

[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): No class. Just that, and a bit more fluid, even weak rooibos counts. Sister, book bloods this week for the potassium and the kidney numbers, and a review here in two weeks.
[SEG0045] person_4 (NURSE): Ja, I'll do the bloods for Thursday morning, and the review in two weeks.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Thursday then. Can we go? I'm finished.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can go. Take it easy this afternoon.

spec.situation: Older person with calf cramps at night for two months; takes a water tablet; drinks little water; magnesium from the shop; blood tests for potassium planned; stretching advice.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
